prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and made it a precision probe of relativity and fundamental constants.

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean, controllable quantum experiment in which every physical detail matters. Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping a very large number of atoms in the interrogation, and Ye's group turned the idea into clocks with 1e-18 accuracy and stability. The result is a discovery-level change in what can be measured: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of variation of constants, and relativistic geodesy. The effect has been reproduced and surpassed across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and the SI second is being reconsidered because of it. Five of eight members ranked it, three of them first, and it has the cleanest two-name attribution on the shortlist. The science is mature and recognition is timely.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is an incremental extension of earlier recognised metrology: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize for measuring single quantum systems, which includes the Wineland ion clock. A reader could also say it rewards an instrument rather than a new phenomenon, and that Lemonde, Hollberg and the single-ion clock community have real priority claims. I think the magic-wavelength concept is distinct, but I am relying on memory of the priority history and have not verified it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a textbook measurement advance, but notes that Ye's frequency-comb and laser-stabilisation work partly lies in territory already recognised in 2005, and prefers one theorist and two experimentalists for the lattice-simulation candidate.
responses.response: I agree the 2005 overlap is the right concern, and it is why I would make the citation about the magic-wavelength lattice clock and not about combs or stabilised lasers, so that Ye is credited for taking that clock to record accuracy and for the redshift tests. The same logic does not rescue B012, where I find the theory-experiment allocation among Zoller, Cirac, Greiner and Bloch harder to settle than the Katori-Ye split.

responses.point: Lindroth, who knows atomic physics well, supports B049 as building on earlier comb and cooling prizes while adding something new, and puts B040 low (rank 8) because the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits reduces the timeliness of another circuit award.
responses.response: I agree with her on B040, and I move it down from my opening rank 2 for that reason, although I think the physics is outstanding. A prize for circuit QED within a year of the 2025 award would look like honouring one community twice, and the Girvin attribution gap does not help. She raises single-ion clocks as a lineage issue. The lattice clock's use of many atoms at once is what gives the stability gain, so I see it as a distinct step and not a refinement of the Wineland clock.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B010 (gamma-ray burst afterglows) first and the IceCube neutrino candidate B047 second as instrument-driven discoveries, and ranks the lattice clock sixth, citing the 2005 comb lineage and the still-pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I respect the instrument argument, and the afterglow case is scientifically clean. My doubt is attribution: the optical identification involved van Paradijs, who has died, and Kulkarni's role rests on follow-up, so a three-name set looks fragile. On timing, I do not think the SI redefinition has to be completed first. The prize is for the physics, and that has been confirmed by independent laboratories and is not in doubt. I defer to Pearce and Danielsson on astroparticle questions, but with a single credited name B047 seems to me to under-represent AMANDA and the detector builders.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because flat bands were predicted by theory before the 2018 experiments, and values that theory-experiment link; he also sees the pairing mechanism as unsettled but the discovery as robust.
responses.response: I take the theory-experiment point seriously, and B009 is my preferred alternative outside AMO. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the Jarillo-Herrero experiments is a model case. My hesitation is the one I raised in my own ballot: the nature of the superconducting and correlated states is not settled, and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto have an earlier flat-band claim. I defer to the condensed-matter members on how settled the interpretation is. Compared with the clock, the discovery is less finished, but I would not oppose it if the condensed-matter colleagues are confident.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active-matter hydrodynamics first as a clear case of simple mechanisms explaining collective behaviour far from equilibrium, and acknowledges that credit extends beyond three people.
responses.response: The Toner-Tu result on long-range order in two dimensions is an elegant theoretical discovery, and I find the argument persuasive. I have no detailed knowledge of the experimental verification and defer to him on that. The point I would press is the one he raises himself: the credit is spread over Marchetti, Prost, Julicher and others, and the test of the exact exponents is only partial, so I would want to see more evidence of robustness across experiments before it competes with an established, multiply confirmed result.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and other groups (Lemonde, Hollberg, single-ion clocks); I have not independently verified the history.
Whether a second part (for example B047 with Halzen) should be added to the prize, which would depend on how colleagues judge attribution and maturity there.
How much the 2025 prize on circuit quantum behaviour should weigh against B040, which I otherwise find scientifically strong.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work in superconducting circuits, and I am close to several groups on B040 (Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Blais and Yale and ETH colleagues), and Chalmers colleagues Delsing and Wilson overlap with that wider community, so I should recuse myself from any decision on B040 and I defer on its attribution. I have no apparent connection to Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted candidates in B049, B012, B009, B026, B047, B010, B011 or B029 from the provided profile.
